description: Dillahunty argues that New Testament miracle narratives, including the resurrection, merely report supernatural claims and cannot independently establish those claims as true.
critique: Strongest feature: Dillahunty sharply distinguishes faithfully transmitting resurrection and healing narratives from independently confirming their supernatural contents, directly confronting Knechtle’s manuscript-reliability argument and cumulative resurrection indicia. Principal limitation: His categorical assertion that a story is not evidence unjustifiably collapses potentially limited testimonial evidence into evidential nullity, without examining provenance, source independence, corroboration, or Knechtle’s cumulative presentation. Live burden: He still must demonstrate why the cited witness reports, conversions, empty tomb, immediate proclamation, costly adherence, and early-church emergence collectively remain insufficient, rather than relying exclusively on the report-event distinction. Locked score: The score of 78 appropriately rewards direct reply contact, lucid burden relevance, and coherent resistance to textual self-validation, while withholding credit because evidential warrant and charitable calibration lag behind responsiveness and precision.
